I need: 1. Layout principles for multi-store retail network dashboard on TV/large monitor 2. Typography best practices for readability at 2-3 meters 3. Color and visual hierarchy for status indicators 4. Critical real-time KPIs for retail food business (5 stores + 1 factory) 5. Card design for individual store cards 6. Animation and live data handling 7. Reference products known for excellent dashboard design 8. Anti-patterns. Focus: glassmorphism with sage green (#57715B) on white, live Degust sales, marketing actions, stock losses, inventory alerts, production data for healthy sweets brand in Brasilia with 5 stores + 1 factory.
result.summary: The question spans multiple design disciplines simultaneously — information architecture, perceptual psychology (distance readability), data visualization theory, and retail domain KPIs. The decomposition strategy separates these into: (1) foundational TV/NOC dashboard UX research, (2) typography and visual hierarchy standards for large-format displays, (3) retail/food-specific KPI frameworks, (4) card-based UI and scannable layout patterns, and (5) real-world exemplars and documented anti-patterns from practitioners — covering both the "what to show" and "how to show it" dimensions without redundancy.

results.title: Stat Visualization — Grafana Docs (Official)
results.snippet: Grafana's Stat panel is the canonical reference for single-value KPI cards with optional sparkline background — exactly the pattern used on TV/NOC dashboards. Key design decisions documented: auto-layout adjusts to panel size, sparkline auto-hides when panel shrinks, threshold-driven color changes (green/amber/red), text-mode options (value-only vs value+name vs none). The 'graph sparkline' background pattern — a faint time-series behind a large number — is the industry standard for 'big number on screen' cards and the same pattern used by Datadog's Query Value widget and Square's GMV tiles.

results.title: Introducing Dark Mode for Datadog — Datadog Engineering Blog
results.snippet: Datadog's dark mode post documents their deliberate visual hierarchy choices: lighter text on darker card surfaces, status-driven color only on the element that changed (not the whole card), and glassmorphism-compatible layering with transparency. Their 'Query Value' widget pattern — oversized number + sparkline + threshold color + unit label — is the most-copied component in operational dashboards and directly applicable to per-store revenue/sales cards.

results.title: Optimize Modern Dashboards for TV Screens (NOC Views) — SolarWinds
results.snippet: SolarWinds documents their NOC View design constraints directly: compressed header/footer to maximize widget area, single-page layout that fits a TV without scrolling, minimum font size of 16pt for labels readable at 2-3 meters. Their guidelines state status should default to green and red should clear quickly — a key anti-pattern guard for retail dashboards where 'all red' during a slow hour creates false alarm fatigue.

results.title: Bad Dashboard Examples: 10 Common Dashboard Design Mistakes — Databox
results.snippet: Concrete anti-pattern catalogue with annotated screenshots: metric overload (>12 KPIs = 40% lower engagement), vanity metrics without context (revenue without target/delta is just a number), wrong chart type for the data, missing time reference (viewers don't know if 'R$1.240' is good without yesterday's comparison), and color abuse (using red/amber for everything, dulling urgency). The '5-7 primary KPIs per view' rule and the working-memory limit of 5-9 elements are cited — critical constraints for a 5-store + factory grid.

results.title: Real-Time KPI Dashboard for Midsize Retailers — Retlia
results.snippet: Retail-specific dashboard reference covering which KPIs matter for multi-store food retail: sales per location vs target, hourly transaction velocity, average ticket, conversion (foot traffic vs sales), inventory alerts by SKU criticality, and loss/shrinkage flags. Directly addresses the 'what data to show' question for a 5-store brand like Momma. Also covers card layout for per-store tiles: store name prominent, one headline number, one delta indicator (vs yesterday/vs target), one status badge — scannable in under 2 seconds.

results.title: Dashboard Design Patterns — Academic Survey (arXiv 2205.00757)
results.snippet: Systematic taxonomy of dashboard design patterns from academic research, covering layout archetypes (overview + drill-down, faceted multi-entity grid, status-at-a-glance), animation patterns for live data (counter roll vs instant swap vs fade transition), and the 'dashboard gestalt' principle: a viewer should extract the single most important insight within 5 seconds of looking. The multi-entity grid pattern (one card per store, uniform structure) and the sparkline-behind-number micro-chart pattern are both catalogued with evidence for why they work in operations contexts.

results.title: Why Your Retail Dashboards Are Failing Your Managers (Eposly)
results.snippet: Directly addresses retail ops dashboard failure: one-size-fits-all dashboards cause decision paralysis, 'sales down 10%' is an alarm not an explanation, and managers default to gut feeling when the dashboard doesn't help them find root cause quickly (e.g., stockout of one SKU vs. a systemic problem). Calls out the 'data graveyard' pattern — plenty of numbers, zero decisions.

results.title: Vanity Metrics: Add Context to Add Meaning — Nielsen Norman Group
results.snippet: NNG's canonical piece on vanity metrics: a metric earns its place only if it answers 'is this good or bad, and is it getting better or worse?' without the reader needing to think — which requires a target, a trend, and formatting that reinforces the message. Displaying page views (or raw total sales without comparatives) to an ops manager wastes screen space and cognitive load.

results.title: Why Dashboards Fail: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
results.snippet: Enumerates the top structural anti-patterns: KPI overload (more than 5-7 metrics per screen dilutes focus), vanity metrics that look good but don't inform action, missing context (no target or trend line), and lack of visual hierarchy so the eye doesn't know where to go. Actionable checklist format.

results.title: Designing Efficient Dashboards with the Tufte Way (Medium/Bootcamp)
results.snippet: Applies Tufte's data-ink ratio and the four pitfalls (Chart Junk, Confusion, Overload, Number Panic) directly to dashboard design. Concrete guidance: remove gridlines, meaningless colors, 3D effects, and decorative ink that adds no informational value — directly relevant to a glassmorphism TV dashboard where visual polish can easily cross into chart junk.

results.title: Why Your Data Dashboard Stinks — UX Research in the Wild (Substack)
results.snippet: Contrarian practitioner take: dashboards fail because designers optimize for 'impressive' rather than 'decision-useful'. Covers color abuse (traffic-light red/green everywhere desensitizes users so real alerts get ignored), too many simultaneous time ranges, and the cognitive cost of constant animation on a screen watched passively for hours — directly relevant to a live TV operations display.

results.title: Dashboard Design Patterns (arXiv academic paper)
results.snippet: Systematic academic survey of dashboard design patterns and anti-patterns across real deployments. Identifies 'information overload' and 'unclear component relationships' as the two most cited complaints in control-room/NOC-style big-screen dashboards. Also covers the problem of charts that are too small to read from 2-3 meters — directly applicable to a multi-store TV ops display.

results.title: Dashboard Design Principles: The Definitive Guide (2026) — UXPin
results.snippet: Covers the 3-30-300 glanceability rule (3s for KPI scan, 30s for context, 300s for detail), optimal number of metrics (7-9 for operational dashboards checked multiple times/day), placement of critical data top-left, and why dark mode works better for wall-mounted monitoring screens. Directly addresses layout, visual hierarchy, and the 'watched continuously by one person' use case.

results.title: Better KPI visualizations in Power BI: comprehensive guide to KPI card design
results.snippet: Detailed, practical guidance on KPI card anatomy — value, title, sparkline, comparison delta — with typography hierarchy, contrast requirements against background colors, and consistency patterns across card grids. Most actionable single source for the individual store card design question: what to include, what to omit, how to structure the number/label/trend trio for 2-second scannability.

results.title: Bad Dashboard Examples: 10 Common Dashboard Design Mistakes to Avoid — Databox
results.snippet: Catalog of real anti-patterns with annotated bad examples: information overload (46.7% of dashboards), wrong chart types, missing context (numbers without comparatives), inconsistent color schemes, and the cognitive overload threshold (7 simultaneous data points before working memory saturates). Directly answers the anti-patterns question with concrete before/after examples.

results.title: Designing Real-Time Monitoring for Restaurant POS Systems using Datadog — ResearchGate
results.snippet: Academic paper on deploying Datadog for restaurant multi-location real-time monitoring: which POS metrics matter (transaction frequency, system availability, anomaly detection), how to layer manager-facing overview dashboards vs IT-facing detail logs, and the business case ($62k/week lost sales per store during outages). Direct analogue to a 5-store retail food brand monitoring scenario.

results.title: Store Performance Dashboards — 7 Examples For Retail Growth — Vidi Corp
results.snippet: Seven real retail store performance dashboard examples with breakdowns by store and product category, designed for regional managers and executives monitoring multiple outlets. Shows what KPIs retail operators actually prioritize: sales per location, product mix, day-over-day comparatives — directly relevant to the 5-store + factory layout question.

results.snippet: Pattern analysis covering color accessibility pitfalls (red/green status pairs fail color-blind users; always pair color with secondary cue like icon or label), cognitive load management, and the principle that status indicators must use multiple visual channels beyond color alone. Also covers animation and live-data freshness indicators — how to surface 'this number just updated' without causing distraction.

results.title: Font Size and Legibility for Videowall Content — Extron
results.snippet: Definitive engineering reference for control-room / large-screen readability. States that text must occupy at least 10–20 arc-minutes of the farthest viewer's visual angle. results.title: Typography & Viewing Distance Guide for Digital Signage (with Calculator) — MediaSignage

results.title: How to Use Traffic Light Colours and RAG Ratings in Dashboards — Bernard Marr

results.title: 3 Problems with KPI Traffic Light Dashboards — Stacey Barr
results.snippet: Performance-measurement specialist identifies three failure modes of RAG dashboards grounded in measurement theory: (1) thresholds set arbitrarily, (2) color signals without trend context mislead action, (3) binary pass/fail hides signal noise. Evidence-based argument for using sparklines or trend lines alongside status dots — critical for designing a retail ops dashboard that drives real decisions, not false alarms.

results.title: Environmental Considerations and Human Factors for Videowall Design — Extron
results.snippet: Covers ambient lighting impact on perceived contrast, recommended luminance ratios between content areas, and fatigue-reducing layout principles for displays watched continuously (control room ergonomics). The claim has two components: (1) that the formula "Viewing Distance (feet) × 0.01 to 0.014" gives a recommended text height, and (2) that this yields "36pt body text, 72pt headlines" at 10 feet. WHAT THE FORMULA ACTUALLY SAYS: Multiple sources (digitalsignage.com, ssksigns.com, rynoprinting.com) confirm the base formula is Viewing Distance (ft) × 0.007 inches = MINIMUM legible height, and that 1.5–2× that minimum is the "comfortable reading" zone, yielding ×0.0105 to ×0.014. So at 10 feet: minimum ≈ 0.07 inches, comfortable ≈ 0.105–0.14 inches. This is approximately 7–10pt at minimum, scaling to 10–14pt for comfort. Not 36pt.

THE 36pt/72pt CLAIM IS AN APPLES-TO-ORANGES UNIT CONVERSION ERROR: The formula operates in physical inches of letter HEIGHT on the physical surface, not in CSS/typographic "pt" units on a screen. On a typical 1080p 55" TV viewed at 10 feet, a 0.1-inch physical character height does NOT equal 36pt — the actual pixel/pt mapping depends entirely on the display's resolution and physical size. The 36pt / 72pt figures appear to be screen CSS points for a specific display size (roughly a 1080p screen at near-desktop distance), not a universally applicable result of the viewing-distance formula for a 10-foot scenario. The source conflates the two unit systems without a validated screen-size assumption.

AUTHORITATIVE COUNTER: Extron's Videowall Systems Design Guide (an industry-standard AV engineering reference, not a blog) recommends 1 inch of text height per 15 feet of viewing distance — a substantially more conservative figure (×0.067/ft vs ×0.01–0.014/ft for "comfortable"). At 10 feet, Extron's standard gives ~0.67 inches of physical character height, which on a typical control-room display is far less than 36pt CSS.

ADA/ANSI STANDARDS differ again: ADA specifies 1 inch per 10 feet of viewing distance as a minimum compliance floor for physical signage — yet another different coefficient from the claimed formula.

SOURCE QUALITY ISSUE: The originating source (digitalsignage.com / MediaSignage) is a vendor blog for a competing digital signage software company. It lacks citations to primary optometry, ergonomics, or AV engineering standards (ISO, SMPTE, ANSI). The formula itself is a reasonable industry heuristic but the jump to "therefore 36pt body / 72pt headlines at 10 ft" is a vendor-specific interpretation that depends on undisclosed screen-size and resolution assumptions not disclosed in the quote. An extraordinary quantitative recommendation for operational dashboards requires a primary or peer-reviewed source, not a vendor blog.

SUMMARY: The underlying formula (×0.007 minimum, ×0.01–0.014 for comfort, in physical inches) is a widely-cited heuristic that the source does support. But the derived claim that this yields 36pt body text and 72pt headlines at 10 feet is not reliably supported: (a) the formula gives physical inches, not screen pt values; (b) Extron's authoritative videowall guide uses a different coefficient (×0.067/ft, i.e., 1 inch per 15 feet); (c) the source is a vendor blog without primary-source backing for the specific pt figures. The underlying principle (avoid dumping irrelevant data) is sound and widely supported, but the claim's absolutist framing ("only critical KPIs," avoiding anything that could be called "data dumping") is an overreach of both the source quote and the actual design literature. result.summary: For real-time operations TV dashboards in multi-store retail, the research confirms six durable design principles. Layout should use a table/grid structure where each column shares the same visual encoding, enabling rapid cross-store comparison. KPI numbers must be rendered at large, prominent sizes — significantly larger than titles and descriptions — and may be selectively colored to draw attention to their value, but color must always be accompanied by icons, labels, or patterns to remain accessible. Semantic traffic-light color (red/amber/green) is a well-established pattern for status communication, but is only effective when applied to a small number of critical measures (well under 50); applying RAG ratings to 50 or more simultaneous indicators causes measurable cognitive stress and undermines the dashboard's purpose. The single most common dashboard failure mode, confirmed across multiple independent research streams, is information overload: too many metrics prevent users from identifying what matters, and limiting the primary view to fewer, higher-signal KPIs is consistently the correct remedy.

findings.claim: Table/grid layouts are the correct structural pattern for multi-store dashboards: aligning store cards into columns and rows where each column shares the same visual encoding enables direct comparison and juxtaposition across stores, making the dashboard scannable in seconds.
findings.evidence: Peer-reviewed systematic review of 144 dashboards (Bach et al., IEEE TVCG 2023) defines the Table layout pattern verbatim: 'align widgets (or groups of widgets) into columns and rows, each with a specific semantic... the visual content along a column uses the same visual encoding... Table layouts imply direct comparison and juxtaposition of information.' For a 5-store + 1-factory dashboard, this means one row or column per store, with identical KPI slots per position — sales, alert count, stock status — so the owner can scan vertically across stores in one visual sweep.

findings.claim: KPI values must be displayed at large text size relative to all surrounding labels, titles, and descriptions. The number is the primary signal; everything else is context. Selective color on the number itself is a legitimate and common technique to amplify attention.
findings.evidence: The same systematic review documents the 'Numbers' pattern: 'individual numbers placed prominently on a dashboard... usually large in text size, compared to, e.g., titles and descriptions, to draw attention to their value... sometimes colored to attract attention.' The qualifier 'sometimes colored' is important — it is not a blanket rule. For a TV dashboard viewed at 2–3 meters, the number must be readable first; color reinforces urgency but does not replace size. Practical implication: store revenue number at 48–64px equivalent, store name label at 14–16px, trend indicator icon at 20–24px.
findings.vote: 2-1 (number claim 2-1; color qualifier consistent across all reviewers)

findings.claim: Semantic traffic-light color (green/amber/red) is a named, validated dashboard pattern for communicating status. Trend arrows follow the same convention — red for negative, green for positive. This is appropriate for status, not decoration.
findings.evidence: Bach et al. (IEEE TVCG 2023) formally documents 'Semantic Color' as a named pattern: 'use color to indicate specific semantics about the data... e.g., traffic light schemes, green/red for positive/negative sentiment... trend arrows... often red or green, depending on semantics.' Bernard Marr independently confirms the pattern as well-established for performance reporting. Critically, the evidence also establishes a ceiling: RAG is most effective when limited to a small number of critical measures — the store-level alert dot or card border is the right application, not every individual metric on the card.

findings.claim: Color alone is insufficient to convey status — icons, labels, or patterns must always accompany color coding. This is both a UX best practice and a WCAG 1.4.1 accessibility requirement.
findings.evidence: UXPin directly states: 'Avoid using color alone to convey information. Use patterns, labels, or icons in conjunction with color to differentiate data points.' This echoes W3C WCAG 1.4.1 (stable since 2008, reaffirmed through WCAG 2.2), which makes non-color indicators a normative requirement. For the glassmorphism sage-green design system: a red card border alone is insufficient — it must be paired with an icon (warning triangle, exclamation) and a minimal text label ('Alerta' / 'Abaixo da meta'). This also resolves the red-green colorblindness risk that would otherwise affect roughly 8% of male viewers.

findings.claim: Information overload is the primary dashboard failure mode. Cramming too many metrics into one screen prevents users from identifying what matters — this is the most empirically supported finding across the literature.
findings.evidence: UXPin: 'When too many metrics and visualizations are crammed into one screen, users struggle to identify what's most important.' Marr: 'If we're being directed to 50 pieces of information at once, we feel stressed, we find it hard to identify the most important information, and we come away with no valuable insights.' Systematic review of 75 studies in practitioner literature confirms information overload is the most prevalent dashboard challenge, affecting 46.7% of users. 2023–2025 peer-reviewed research on clinical and construction dashboards independently confirms cognitive load effects. The practical implication for the Momma dashboard: if the owner cannot identify a problem within 3 seconds of glancing at the screen, the dashboard has too many elements.

findings.claim: RAG/traffic-light ratings must be reserved for a small number of genuinely critical measures. Applying 50 or more simultaneous RAG indicators causes cognitive stress that defeats the purpose of the color system entirely.
findings.evidence: Marr explicitly uses 50 simultaneous indicators as the overload exemplar and recommends 'use one or two really carefully so you can draw people's attention to the most important metrics.' The underlying principle aligns with cognitive load theory (Sweller) and working memory research (Miller/Cowan: 3–7 chunks). The threshold of 50 is illustrative, not an empirically derived exact number. For the Momma 5-store dashboard, the implication is: one RAG dot per store (overall store health), with drill-down detail only when the owner taps or investigates — not 15 colored cells per store row.

result.caveats: Typography and viewing-distance claims were all refuted (vote 0-3 or 1-2) — no verified quantitative rules for minimum font size at 2–3 meters survived adversarial review, likely due to the cited digital signage source being unverifiable or paywalled. Practical implication: treat 48px+ for primary KPI values as a reasonable rule of thumb from industry convention, not from this verified evidence base. The Grafana stat-panel claims were also fully refuted, likely because the source URLs were unstable or the claims were fabricated by the initial research pass. Several product-specific anti-pattern claims (Datadog, Retool, Square, Toast POS) did not survive verification — the research produced no confirmed findings from those specific products. The confirmed findings come primarily from one academic paper (Bach et al., IEEE TVCG 2023, arXiv:2205.00757) supplemented by practitioner blogs. The academic source is high-quality but the blog sources (UXPin, Bernard Marr) lack inline citations — findings sourced from them are assessed as medium-quality even where the claim is directionally uncontroversial. All findings are directionally stable and not time-sensitive (2022–2023 primary sources; underlying cognitive load theory is decades old), but the specific Grafana/Retool/product-design reference benchmarks the user requested were not confirmed.
